strengths: BiAlign offers a clear, NLP-relevant extension to knowledge distillation: matching teacher preferences over demonstration subsets alongside token-level output distributions. The modification requires no additional inference-time component.

The evaluation examines transfer from CrossFit to diverse held-out benchmarks and includes fine-tuning, continual pretraining, and output-distillation baselines. BiAlign achieves the highest reported score on all five benchmarks, averaging 30.2 versus 29.2 for Output-Align and 29.4 for fine-tuning.

The equations, pseudocode, and diagrams communicate the central method effectively. Experiments varying subset count, demonstration count, and source-task selection provide useful initial sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: The reliability of the gains is insufficiently established. Improvements over the strongest baseline for each benchmark are only 0.2–0.7 percentage points, with no reported variability across training runs, confidence intervals, or paired significance analysis. HumanEval's increase from 14.6 to 15.2 corresponds to approximately one additional solved problem among 164. These results provide limited support for strong claims about consistent superiority and preservation of zero-shot abilities.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism. BiAlign introduces additional subset contexts and teacher evaluations alongside preference ranking. Comparing against output distillation on those same subsets would help distinguish the ranking contribution from context augmentation and additional computation. Comparisons with simpler ranking objectives and measurements of held-out teacher–student ranking agreement are also missing.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the supplied basic hyperparameters. The manuscript omits optimizer and learning-rate schedule details, maximum sequence length and truncation behavior, and sufficiently precise training-prompt construction. Equation 3 also leaves zero student-score ranges and tied teacher preferences unspecified. No implementation link is provided, and the appendix contains only a heading.

HumanEval reporting needs clarification. With one greedy completion for each of 164 problems, the reported FT score of 14.2% and C-Pretrain score of 13.2% cannot be obtained as rounded single-run success rates. If results average multiple runs or use another aggregation procedure, that procedure and its variability must be documented.

Broader evidence is limited to one teacher–student pair, Llama 2-13B to Llama 2-7B, without training-cost measurements for the additional subset evaluations. The source-diversity analysis also does not establish that training volume is held constant. These limit generality and interpretation; the more decisive reasons for requesting revision are the unresolved empirical controls, uncertainty, and reproducibility gaps.
